patient.chief_complaint: Progressive memory loss over the past 18 to 24 months with increasing forgetfulness and difficulty managing daily tasks
patient.history_present_illness: A 71-year-old right-handed retired male middle school teacher presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by his wife for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties. His wife, who serves as the primary informant, reports that she first noticed subtle changes approximately 18 to 24 months ago, shortly after his retirement. He retired at age 69 primarily because of progressive bilateral hearing loss, but his wife notes that the memory difficulties became apparent around the same time and have been gradually worsening independent of his hearing issues. The earliest symptoms included repeating questions he had just asked, forgetting the content of recent conversations, and misplacing everyday items such as his wallet and keys. Over the following months, the memory lapses became more frequent and noticeable. He began forgetting appointments, including a longstanding monthly lunch with a former colleague. On two occasions in the past six months, he left the gas stove on after cooking, which prompted significant concern from his wife. He previously managed all of the household finances, including bill payments and tax preparation, but approximately eight months ago his wife discovered several unpaid utility bills and took over these responsibilities. He has difficulty following the plots of television programs and often asks what is happening during shows he has watched from the beginning. He frequently loses track of the day of the week and has occasionally appeared confused about the time of day, remarking that time seems to move strangely. His wife also describes a change in his personality: he has become more withdrawn and apathetic, declining invitations from friends and spending more time sitting quietly at home. He has expressed frustration and awareness of his declining memory, telling his wife on multiple occasions that he feels as though he is losing his mind. He continues to dress and bathe independently, though his wife has noticed he occasionally wears the same clothes on consecutive days. He can still prepare simple meals and navigate familiar routes in the neighborhood without getting lost, though his wife recently began accompanying him on errands as a precaution. There is no history of sudden stepwise decline, fluctuating awareness, visual hallucinations, falls, tremor, or gait disturbance. He has not experienced any episodes of confusion associated with fever or illness. He denies depressed mood, though his wife notes the social withdrawal. He sleeps well without evidence of REM sleep behavior disorder. There have been no episodes of urinary incontinence. His appetite has remained stable.

clinical_assessment.impression: Cognitive impairment documented on a validated bedside instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile, and delayed recall that does not recover with cueing — a storage rather than a retrieval deficit, which is the pattern of Alzheimer pathology. The informant history and the loss of instrumental independence establish decline from a previous level and place the syndrome at the dementia rather than the mild threshold. This assessment is the step that makes the syndrome measurable; imaging and biomarkers then attribute it.

output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly amnestic profile with multi-domain involvement. Episodic memory is markedly impaired: CVLT-II delayed recall at the 3rd percentile and recognition memory at the 12th percentile indicate a storage-type deficit. Semantic fluency (Category Fluency — Animals: 10 words/minute) and confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 15th percentile) are below expected norms. Executive function and processing speed (Trail Making A and B, 18th–22nd percentile) and visuoconstructive ability (Rey Complex Figure Copy, 30th percentile) are within low-normal range. Screening scores: MMSE 22/30, MoCA 18/30. Mood screening does not support a primary depressive etiology (GDS 4/15). Profile is consistent with amnestic mild cognitive impairment, multi-domain type

results.title: Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer's Disease
results.authors: van Dyck CH, Swanson CJ, et al.
results.summary: Phase 3 trial (CLARITY AD) demonstrated that lecanemab, an anti-amyloid antibody, reduced clinical decline by 27% over 18 months in early AD (MCI to mild dementia) compared to placebo. ARIA (amyloid-related imaging abnormalities) occurred in 21.3% of lecanemab-treated patients. FDA approved January 2023.

results.title: Donepezil and Memantine for Moderate-to-Severe Alzheimer's Disease
results.summary: DOMINO-AD trial showed continued benefit of donepezil in moderate-to-severe AD. Starting donepezil in early disease remains standard of care. Memantine showed additional benefit when added to donepezil in moderate-to-severe stages.

results.title: 2023 Appropriate Use Recommendations for Lecanemab
results.authors: Cummings J, Rabinovici GD, et al.
results.journal: Journal of Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease
results.summary: Appropriate use criteria require biomarker-confirmed amyloid pathology, early-stage disease (MCI or mild dementia), baseline MRI without extensive ARIA risk factors, and informed shared decision-making. APOE ε4 homozygotes and patients on anticoagulants have higher ARIA risk.

output.summary: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) have demonstrated symptomatic benefits in randomized controlled trials of early Alzheimer's disease. Disease-modifying anti-amyloid therapies (lecanemab, donanemab) have demonstrated slowing of clinical decline in biomarker-confirmed early-stage disease. Patient selection criteria for anti-amyloid therapies include biomarker confirmation (amyloid PET or CSF), baseline MRI screening, and assessment of ARIA risk factors including APOE genotype.

output.proposed: Donepezil 5 mg once daily at bedtime, titrating to 10 mg after 4-6 weeks
interactions: Donepezil + Amlodipine: No clinically significant interaction. Both are metabolized by CYP3A4 but no dose adjustment needed.
Donepezil + Tamsulosin: No significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Both may cause dizziness; advise caution with positional changes.
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to donepezil or piperidine derivatives
warnings: Cholinergic effects: may cause bradycardia — monitor heart rate, particularly given concurrent amlodipine
GI side effects (nausea, diarrhea, anorexia) are common, especially during dose titration
May exacerbate urinary obstruction — monitor given history of BPH and concurrent tamsulosin
May lower seizure threshold — monitor clinically
May exacerbate pulmonary conditions due to cholinergic effects — no active pulmonary disease in this patient
output.formulary_status: On formulary, no prior authorization required. Generic available.
alternatives: Rivastigmine patch (4.6 mg/24h, titrate to 13.3 mg/24h) — transdermal delivery may reduce GI side effects
Galantamine ER 8 mg daily, titrate to 16-24 mg — dual mechanism (AChE inhibitor + nicotinic receptor modulator)
Memantine 5 mg daily, titrate to 10 mg twice daily — typically reserved for moderate-to-severe AD, but may be added later

differential.key_features: DLB must be actively excluded by absence of visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, cognitive fluctuations, and REM sleep behavior disorder; biomarkers and (when needed) DaTscan can distinguish if features emerge
FTD typically presents with prominent personality change, disinhibition, or progressive aphasia rather than amnesia; positive amyloid biomarkers further argue against FTLD pathology
No significant cerebrovascular burden on MRI and the gradual amnestic course is not stepwise — pure VCI is unlikely
Insidious course over months to years with disproportionate delayed-recall impairment and limited benefit from cueing is not typical of pseudodementia

differential.diagnosis: Reversible metabolic, endocrine, or sleep-related cognitive impairment
differential.key_features: Screening labs exclude hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, and HIV; the progressive amnestic profile would not normalize with treatment of any of these alone

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed clinical history from patient and informant, including timeline, cognitive domains affected, functional decline, mood, sleep, and medication review
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Gradually progressive cognitive change with informant-confirmed functional impairment in IADLs

optimal_actions.action: Perform bedside cognitive assessment (MMSE and/or MoCA) and detailed neurological examination
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Objective cognitive impairment on MoCA more sensitive than MMSE; non-focal neurological exam (or variant-specific findings — visuospatial in PCA, language in lvPPA, behavioral in frontal AD)

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis to patient and family, discuss prognosis, advance directives, and driving / safety assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and caregiver engaged in care planning; safety concerns (driving, finances, medication management) addressed

optimal_actions.action: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Impairment documented on a validated instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile and informant-confirmed decline from a previous level, staged by whether independence in instrumental activities is preserved (mild cognitive impairment) or lost (dementia)

optimal_actions.action: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Amnestic profile with disproportionate impairment of delayed recall and limited benefit from cueing, plus involvement of at least one other cognitive domain

optimal_actions.action: Order the reviewed cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible mimics (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis) excluded; identify and address co-morbid metabolic factors

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral medial-temporal / hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA grade 2-3) with temporoparietal cortical volume loss

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CSF Alzheimer biomarkers as the single optional biological-confirmation route
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reduced Aβ42 (or reduced Aβ42/40 ratio) with elevated p-tau supporting A+T+ profile consistent with Alzheimer pathology

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, or galantamine)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No clinically significant interactions; counsel on GI side effects and bradycardia risk

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect / herniation risk, particularly in older patients

critical_actions: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate; HIV/RPR per risk)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia/volumetric protocol
Quantify cognitive impairment with a standardized cognitive battery (MoCA at minimum; formal neuropsychological testing when feasible)
Assess safety: driving, medication management, finances, and need for caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family

Consider the single case-designated optional biomarker route if biological confirmation would change management or uncertainty remains when MRI is equivocal or when an atypical AD variant is suspected
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not attribute symptoms entirely to normal aging, depression, or sleep apnea without completing the dementia workup
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
key_reasoning_points: Definite hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI with a multi-domain amnestic cognitive profile is sufficient to make a clinical diagnosis of probable AD by NIA-AA 2011 criteria
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not used to make the diagnosis; an E3/E4 or E4/E4 result is supportive but neither sufficient nor required for diagnosis
Low-normal B12 should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before being dismissed as a non-contributor
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy in mild-to-moderate AD; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease
